title: FDA Expanded Access and Post-Trial Continued Access to Investigational Drugs: Sponsor Obligations Under 21 CFR 312, FDA Guidance and ICH E6(R3)
summary: How FDA expanded access under 21 CFR 312 Subpart I differs from post-trial continued access, and what FDA guidance and ICH E6(R3) expect of sponsors.
body_markdown:
## FDA expanded access and post-trial continued access to investigational drugs: what 21 CFR 312, FDA guidance and ICH E6(R3) expect of sponsors


In the US, access to an investigational drug outside a development trial sits on two separate tracks. **Expanded access** is governed by 21 CFR Part 312 Subpart I and FDA's expanded access guidances. **Continued access for former trial participants** is generally handled under the development IND as a protocol exception or a continuation (extension) protocol, not as expanded access. ICH E6(R3) does not create a free-standing post-trial access obligation in the text cited here. It does set GCP expectations on uninterrupted supply, continuation of treatment, medical care after participation, follow-up and what participants are told. This article covers each layer and where they meet.


### The regulatory framework: 21 CFR 312 Subpart I


#### Scope and definitions


Subpart I applies to investigational new drugs, and to approved drugs whose availability is limited by a REMS, when the primary purpose is to diagnose, monitor or treat a patient's disease or condition. Its stated aim is access for patients with serious diseases or conditions who have no comparable or satisfactory alternative therapy[205](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.300) .


Two definitions in 21 CFR 312.300(b) set eligibility:


- **Immediately life-threatening disease or condition:** a stage of disease in which there is a reasonable likelihood that death will occur within months, or in which premature death is likely without early treatment[206](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.300) .
- **Serious disease or condition:** a disease or condition associated with morbidity that substantially affects day-to-day functioning. Short-lived, self-limiting morbidity is usually not enough, but morbidity need not be irreversible if it is persistent or recurrent. Seriousness is a clinical judgment based on effects on survival, day-to-day functioning, or the likelihood of progression if untreated[207](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.300)[208](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.300) .


#### General criteria for every expanded access use (312.305(a))


FDA must determine all three of the following before any expanded access use proceeds:


1. The patient or patients have a serious or immediately life-threatening disease or condition, and there is no comparable or satisfactory alternative therapy[39](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) .
2. The potential patient benefit justifies the potential risks, and those risks are not unreasonable in the context of the disease or condition[40](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) .
3. Providing the drug will not interfere with the initiation, conduct or completion of clinical investigations that could support marketing approval of the expanded access use, and will not otherwise compromise its potential development[41](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) .


The third criterion connects expanded access to post-trial planning. Access programs are judged partly on whether they protect the development program.


#### Submission content (312.305(b))


An expanded access submission is required for each type of expanded access. It may be a new IND or a protocol amendment to an existing IND, and required information may be supplied by reference to an existing IND if its sponsor grants a right of reference[42](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) . The submission includes:


- Form FDA 1571
- the rationale for use, including the therapeutic options ordinarily available or why the investigational drug is preferable
- patient-selection criteria, or for an individual patient the disease or condition, recent medical history and previous treatments
- method of administration, dose and duration
- a description of the manufacturing facility and CMC information adequate to ensure identity, quality, purity and strength[43](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305)
- pharmacology and toxicology information adequate to conclude the drug is reasonably safe at the proposed dose and duration
- the clinical procedures, laboratory tests or other monitoring needed to evaluate effects and minimize risk[44](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305)


The submission and its mailing cover must be plainly marked "EXPANDED ACCESS SUBMISSION." For a treatment IND or treatment protocol, the applicable box on Form FDA 1571 must also be checked[45](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) .


### The three categories of expanded access


FDA's April 2026 final guidance, *Expanded Access to Investigational Drugs for Treatment Use: Questions and Answers* , groups submissions into three categories: individual patient expanded access, including emergency use; intermediate-size patient populations; and treatment INDs or treatment protocols for widespread use[80](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=80)[81](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=81)[82](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=82) . Separately, it distinguishes new expanded access INDs from protocols submitted to existing INDs[83](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=83) .


Element Individual patient (312.310) Intermediate-size population (312.315) Treatment IND / treatment protocol (312.320)


Added criteria beyond 312.305(a) Physician determines the probable risk from the drug is no greater than the probable risk from the disease; FDA determines the patient cannot obtain the drug under another IND or protocol[96](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.310) Enough safety evidence to justify a trial of roughly the expected number of patients, plus at least preliminary clinical evidence of effectiveness or a plausible pharmacologic effect[215](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315)[216](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315) Drug is in a controlled trial under an IND designed to support marketing for the use, or all clinical trials have been completed; sponsor is actively pursuing marketing approval with due diligence[108](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.320)[109](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.320)


Evidence standard Physician and FDA judgment as above[96](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.310) As above[215](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315)[216](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315) Serious condition: sufficient clinical evidence of safety and effectiveness, ordinarily phase 3 data, though compelling phase 2 data may suffice. Immediately life-threatening condition: a reasonable basis to conclude the drug may be effective and would not expose patients to an unreasonable and significant risk, ordinarily phase 3 or phase 2 data, though more preliminary evidence may suffice[110](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.320)


Typical situations A single patient, including emergencies[95](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.310) Drug not being developed (for example, a disease too rare to recruit for); patients who cannot join an ongoing trial because of eligibility criteria, closed enrollment or geography; approved products unavailable for safety reasons, for failure to meet approval conditions, or because of a shortage[211](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315)[212](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315)[213](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315) Widespread use[107](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.320)


Key safeguards Generally one course of therapy for a specified duration unless FDA expressly authorizes multiple courses or chronic therapy[99](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.310) ; written summary of results, including adverse effects, at the end of treatment[100](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.310) ; FDA may require sponsor monitoring for extended use[101](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.310) FDA reviews whether continued access is appropriate at the IND annual report[221](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315) ; sponsor monitors protocol compliance[225](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315) Sponsor monitors physician compliance with the protocol and investigator regulations[112](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.320)


Escalation Many similar requests may prompt FDA to ask for a 312.315 or 312.320 submission[102](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.310) As enrollment grows, FDA may ask for a 312.320 submission[224](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315) Not applicable


For intermediate-size access, the sponsor must state whether the drug is being developed. If it is not, the sponsor explains why it cannot currently be developed for the use and under what circumstances it could be. If the drug is in a clinical trial, the sponsor explains why these patients cannot enroll and under what circumstances it would run a trial in them[218](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315)[219](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315)[220](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315) . FDA in turn considers whether a clinical study of the use is possible, or whether access is interfering with development[222](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315)[223](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315) .


#### Emergency use


If treatment must begin before a written submission can be made, FDA may authorize use without one, and the reviewing official may do so by telephone[103](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.310) . Requests may be made by telephone, fax or other electronic communication to CBER's Office of Communication, Outreach and Development for CBER-regulated biologics, to CDER's Division of Drug Information for other drugs, or to the FDA Emergency Call Center after hours[104](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.310) . The physician or sponsor must explain how the use will meet 312.305 and 312.310 and agree to submit the expanded access submission within 15 working days of FDA's authorization[105](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.310) .


FDA authorization is still required before treatment begins. Prior IRB approval is not required for emergency use, but the IRB must be notified within 5 working days[187](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=187)[88](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=88) . Emergency treatment may start after authorization and before FDA receives the written submission, including the letter of authorization[188](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=188) .


### Roles: who is the sponsor and what each party owes


21 CFR 312.305(c) assigns subpart D responsibilities by role:


- A licensed physician under whose immediate direction the drug is administered or dispensed is an **investigator**[47](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) .
- Whoever submits the expanded access IND or protocol is a **sponsor**[48](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) .
- A physician who does both is a **sponsor-investigator** and carries both sets of obligations[49](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) .


The 2026 Q&A confirms that a company can also sponsor expanded access. It permits company-submitted individual emergency-use INDs or protocols (one submission per patient). For multiple patients, FDA generally considers a single company-sponsored intermediate-size or treatment protocol the most efficient approach when the drug is being developed for marketing[78](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=78)[79](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=79) .


**Investigator obligations in all cases:** report adverse drug events to the sponsor, meet Part 50 informed consent requirements, obtain IRB review consistent with Part 56, and keep accurate case histories and drug disposition records under 312.62[50](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) .


**Sponsor obligations in all cases:**


- submit IND safety reports (312.32), and annual reports (312.33) when the IND or protocol continues for a year or longer
- ensure physicians are qualified to administer the drug
- give physicians the information needed to minimize risk and maximize benefit, including the investigator's brochure if one exists
- maintain an effective IND
- keep drug disposition records under 312.57[51](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305)


### Individual patient requests: Form FDA 3926, letters of authorization and IRB review


FDA's guidance *Individual Patient Expanded Access Applications: Form FDA 3926* describes Form 3926 as a streamlined IND application for licensed physicians treating a single patient, including in emergencies. It does not cover the other expanded access categories or medical devices[176](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=176) . Physicians may use Form 3926 or Form 1571 for physician-submitted individual-patient INDs. Individual-patient protocols use Form 1571, and Form 3926 is not intended for commercial sponsors[177](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=177)[178](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=178) .


**Letter of authorization (LOA).** The physician should confirm that the drug can be obtained, then get an LOA from the sponsor of the IND being referenced, such as the manufacturer, so FDA can rely on information already in that IND[184](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=184) . If the IND holder refuses, the physician must include all the information needed to support the expanded access IND[185](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=185) . This is a practical point for companies: the LOA is usually the point at which their access policy is applied.


**IRB review.** Prospective IRB review and approval is required except for emergency use when there is not enough time to obtain it[87](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=87) . For non-emergency individual-patient access, a physician may request a waiver of review at a convened IRB meeting. FDA intends to grant it when the IRB chairperson or another designated member concurs before treatment begins, and the waiver extends to amendments and continuing review[89](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=89) . On Form 3926 the request is made by selecting Field 10.b, and FDA does not send a separate notice granting it[180](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=180) . Only the convened-meeting requirement is waived. Informed consent is still required unless a regulatory exception applies[182](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=182) . FDA's 2023 IRB guidance on individual patient expanded access says review should focus on the particular patient's risks and benefits, and that guidance does not address intermediate-size or treatment-use protocols[90](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=90)[91](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=91) .


**Timing.** A non-emergency Form 3926 IND becomes effective when FDA notifies the physician that treatment may proceed, or 30 days after FDA receives the completed form if no notification is sent[189](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=189)[190](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=190) . Treatment may begin once the IND is effective and the IRB requirement has been met[191](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=191) .


### How FDA uses safety data from expanded access


The 2026 Q&A explains that expanded access adverse event data can identify rare events and safety signals in populations not exposed in trials, and in a very small number of cases have contributed to approved labeling (Q30)[361](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=361) . In Q31, FDA states it does not intend to deny, delay or refuse approval of an NDA or BLA, or place an IND on clinical hold, based solely on an adverse event during expanded access, and that it is unaware of any instance in which such information prevented approval[362](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=362) . FDA interprets these data in context: use is uncontrolled, and patients may have more advanced disease, concomitant therapies or comorbidities[363](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=363) .


### Charging for expanded access (21 CFR 312.8)


Charging requires prior written FDA authorization and a justification of the amount. FDA will withdraw authorization if charging interferes with development or the criteria are no longer met[28](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.8) . The sponsor must reasonably assure FDA that charging will not interfere with development. For a treatment IND or protocol, that assurance includes evidence of sufficient enrollment in ongoing trials, adequate development progress, and development milestones planned for the next year[29](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.8) .


Expanded access category Recoverable costs


Individual patient Direct costs only; administrative costs may not be charged[284](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=284)[285](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=285)


Intermediate-size and treatment IND/protocol Direct costs plus costs of monitoring the IND or protocol, complying with IND reporting requirements, and other administrative costs directly associated with the expanded access use[33](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.8)[286](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=286)


Direct costs are costs specifically and exclusively attributable to the authorized use, such as per-unit manufacturing, acquisition from another manufacturer, and shipping, handling and storage. Indirect costs, such as facilities primarily intended for commercial production, are excluded[31](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.8)[32](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.8) . Under FDA's 2024 guidance *Charging for Investigational Drugs Under an IND: Questions and Answers* , fees paid to a third party administering an intermediate-size or treatment protocol, including that party's profit, may be recovered, and FDA recommends telling patients about any sponsor relationship with the third party[287](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=287) .


The request must include documentation supporting the calculation, with a statement that an independent certified public accountant reviewed and approved it[34](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.8) . A CPA statement is not needed when the sponsor simply passes through a third-party supplier's charge and supports it with the supplier's invoice[292](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=292)[293](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=293) . Authorization lasts one year unless FDA specifies a shorter period[35](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.8) . FDA recommends requesting reauthorization at least 60 days before expiry, and written reauthorization is required before charging beyond the authorized period[296](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=296)[297](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=297) . The one-year limit applies to charging authorization, not to the access itself[140](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=140) .


### Public expanded access policies (FD&C Act section 561A)


A manufacturer or distributor of investigational drugs for serious diseases or conditions must make public its policy for evaluating and responding to expanded access requests[17](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=17) . This covers CDER- and CBER-regulated drugs and biologics. Investigational device manufacturers are not subject to section 561A[18](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=18)[19](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=19) . The policy must include:


- contact information
- procedures for submitting requests
- general criteria for evaluating and responding to individual patient requests
- the expected time to acknowledge receipt of a request
- a hyperlink or other reference to the ClinicalTrials.gov record with expanded access information[20](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=20)


The deadline is the earlier of first initiation of a phase 2 or phase 3 study, or 15 days after breakthrough therapy, fast track or regenerative medicine advanced therapy designation[22](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=22) . FDA reads "initiation" as the start of enrollment and recommends that the company developing the drug, not a distributor, publish the policy[23](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=23) . Posting on the company's website or on the Reagan-Udall Foundation Expanded Access Navigator is acceptable[19](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=19)[24](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=24) . Publishing a policy does not oblige the company to supply the drug. Provision remains voluntary, and FDA cannot compel a sponsor to provide it[25](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=25) .


### Post-trial continued access: how FDA classifies it


The 2026 Q&A separates continued access for trial participants from expanded access. The classification decides which requirements apply.


1.


**Protocol exception (Q34).** Continuing to give the drug to an enrolled patient who no longer meets the inclusion criteria is generally not expanded access, provided the patient is in a trial designed to further development and the patient's results will be included in the analysis. FDA calls this a "protocol exception" covered under the existing IND[408](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=408)[409](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=409) .


2.


**Continuation or extension protocol (Q33).** A continuation protocol, also called an extension trial, lets patients stay on the drug, or cross over from placebo or active control, after the randomized phase ends. Enrollment is typically limited to the original trial's participants[410](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=410) . FDA states:


> "A protocol for which the primary intent is treatment of patients and for which enrollment is limited to patients who participated in the clinical trials to support approval of the investigational drug is considered a continuation protocol and not an expanded access protocol, even though the primary intent is treatment."[411](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=411)


The reasoning is that access has not been expanded beyond the trial population. Treatment-focused continuation protocols generally have a simpler design and fewer requirements than continuation protocols run mainly to collect safety or other data[411](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=411) .


3.


**Patients outside the trial (Q35).** Giving the drug for treatment to a patient who is not enrolled in a trial is generally expanded access, and the expanded access requirements, including an appropriate IND or protocol submission, apply[412](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=412) .


4.


**Labels do not decide the category (Q32).** FDA can identify and review a submission as expanded access even if the sponsor did not call it that. A broadly accessible, late-development open-label study without planned systematic data collection or a design able to evaluate a safety issue will generally be treated as a treatment IND or protocol, and FDA will notify the sponsor[413](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=413) .


Other parts of Subpart I bear on the period after a trial. A treatment IND or protocol is available when all clinical trials of the drug have been completed, as long as the sponsor is actively pursuing marketing approval with due diligence[108](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.320)[109](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.320) . Intermediate-size access covers patients who cannot enter a trial because enrollment has closed[212](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.315) . Where former participants are moved into an expanded access protocol and charged, the 312.8 charging rules and their annual reauthorization apply[139](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=139)[140](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=140) .


### What ICH E6(R3) expects


ICH E6(R3) does not contain a provision that requires sponsors to provide post-trial access to the investigational product. Several provisions still shape how sponsors and investigators handle continuation, the end of participation and the end of a trial.


**Supply and continuation of treatment (sponsor, section 3.15.3).** The sponsor is responsible for supplying the investigational product to investigators, or where appropriate directly to participants, under applicable regulatory requirements[202](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=202) . Section 3.15.3(c)(i) states that the sponsor should:


> "Ensure timely provision of investigational product(s) to the investigator(s) or, where appropriate, to trial participants in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements to avoid any interruption to the trial as well as for the continuation of treatment for participants;"[203](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=203)


This provision names continuation of treatment but does not say whether it applies after the trial or for how long[203](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=203) . ICH E6(R3) Annex 2 (section 3.6.2 of the draft text; Annex 2 reached Step 4 in June 2026) states that the sponsor may arrange to send the investigational product to the participant, for example to the participant's home, in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements[153](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=153) .


**Medical care during and after participation (investigator, section 2.7.1(c)).** "During and following participation in a trial, the investigator/institution should ensure that adequate medical care is provided to a participant for any adverse events, including clinically significant laboratory values, related to the trial"[368](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=368) . The investigator should also inform the participant's primary physician of trial involvement if the participant agrees[369](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=369) .


**Premature termination or suspension.** If a trial is terminated or suspended early, the investigator/institution should promptly inform participants and ensure appropriate therapy and follow-up (section 2.6.1)[370](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=370) . The sponsor should promptly inform investigators, regulators and IRBs/IECs of the reasons and, where appropriate, give investigators information about potential subsequent therapies and follow-up for participants (section 3.17.1)[375](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=375) .


**Informed consent (section 2.8.10).** Consent discussions and materials should explain, as applicable:


- (h) available alternative procedures or courses of treatment and their important potential benefits and risks[322](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=322)
- (i) compensation and/or treatment available for trial-related injury[322](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=322)
- (l) that participation is voluntary and participants may stop the investigational product or withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of benefits to which they are otherwise entitled[152](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=152)
- (m) follow-up procedures for participants who stop the investigational product, withdraw or are discontinued[324](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=324)
- (s) foreseeable circumstances under which participation may be terminated, and (t) the expected duration of participation[379](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=379)
- (v) that trial results and information on the participant's actual treatment, if appropriate, will be made available if the participant wants them, once the sponsor has them[379](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=379)


Section 2.9.3 similarly expects participants, where relevant, to be informed of results and of the treatment they received after unblinding, respecting their preference[201](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=201) . None of those consent elements specifically requires disclosure of post-trial drug availability. In practice, sponsors that plan continuation or expanded access usually address it under the alternatives, duration and follow-up elements.


**Protocol content (Appendix B).** The protocol should describe the expected duration of participation and every trial period, including follow-up (B.4.7)[350](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=350)[351](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=351) ; the follow-up for participants who have stopped the investigational product (B.6(d))[353](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=353) ; and the treatment period and follow-up period for each arm (B.7.1)[354](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=354) . Appendix B does not require the protocol to describe post-trial treatment arrangements.


### Practical implications for sponsors


The points below are drawn from the provisions cited above.


- **Decide the classification early.** Under Q33 to Q35, access limited to former participants of approval-supporting trials can run as a continuation protocol under the development IND, while treatment access for a patient outside a trial is generally expanded access[411](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=411)[412](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=412) . FDA can reclassify a study it sees as a de facto treatment protocol[413](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=413) .
- **Plan supply for continuation.** E6(R3) 3.15.3(c)(i) expects timely supply that avoids interruption and supports continuation of treatment[203](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=203) . Supply forecasts should cover extension and access phases, as well as the CMC information an expanded access submission requires[43](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) .
- **Publish and maintain the 561A policy** by the phase 2/3 or designation trigger, with an acknowledgment timeline and a link to ClinicalTrials.gov[20](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=20)[22](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=22) .
- **Set up for individual requests.** Physicians typically need an LOA to reference the company's IND[184](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=184) . If requests accumulate, FDA may ask for an intermediate-size or treatment protocol[102](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.310) , and FDA generally considers a single company-sponsored protocol more efficient[79](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=79) .
- **Keep the development program protected.** Every expanded access use must not interfere with trials that could support approval[41](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) . For a treatment IND, the sponsor must be pursuing approval with due diligence[109](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.320) , and a charging request for a treatment IND must show enrollment and development progress[29](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.8) .
- **Build end-of-trial obligations into the protocol and consent.** Under E6(R3) these include follow-up for participants who discontinue, appropriate therapy and follow-up if the trial ends early, medical care for trial-related adverse events after participation, and explanation of alternatives and expected duration[353](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=353)[370](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=370)[368](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=368)[322](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=322)[379](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=379) .
- **Carry safety reporting across every route.** IND safety reports and annual reports apply to expanded access[51](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.305) . FDA states that it does not intend to act on a marketing application based solely on an expanded access adverse event[362](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-expanded-access-and-post-trial-continued?showSourceNumber=362) .
